analysis.one_liner: Makes it a federal crime for local police officers to commit murder or manslaughter on the job.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 52 House sponsors, the bill never received a hearing, markup, or vote in the House Judiciary Committee before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let federal prosecutors charge a state or local police officer with federal murder or manslaughter when the officer, working on duty, kills or assaults someone in a way that would be murder or manslaughter under federal law. It applies only to officers in agencies that receive a specific type of federal justice funding. The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee in February 2020 and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: People harmed or killed by on-duty police officers, and their families, would gain a route to federal prosecution when local prosecutors decline to bring charges or local juries acquit. Federal prosecutors are independent of the local police departments they work alongside, which supporters see as the point of the bill.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Families of people killed by police

how_it_helps.text: Creates a new federal crime under title 18 covering on-duty conduct by a state or local law enforcement officer that would be murder (18 U.S.C. 1111) or manslaughter (18 U.S.C. 1112) if committed in federal jurisdiction.
Applies to officers of state and local governments who have arrest authority, are authorized to carry firearms, and whose duties are primarily law enforcement or protection of government officials.

Reaches officers in agencies receiving federal funding under subpart 1 of part E of title I of the Omnibus Crime Control and Safe Streets Act of 1968, which is the main federal grant stream for state and local law enforcement.
Under the bill, the officer is punished as provided for the corresponding murder or manslaughter offense under those federal sections.

analysis.who_pays: Police officers, who would face a new layer of federal criminal exposure for on-duty killings and assaults, and the police unions that represent them. Local agencies could also face pressure as federal grant recipients whose officers fall under the new statute.

drawbacks.text: Officers are already subject to state murder and manslaughter laws, so the bill adds an overlapping federal charge rather than closing a gap in the law; critics could argue this creates duplicate prosecution risk for the same conduct.
The bill covers only officers in agencies receiving one specific federal grant stream, leaving officers in agencies outside that funding stream outside the statute's reach.
A new federal homicide charge for on-duty force could be argued to make officers hesitant to use force in situations where it is legally justified.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is narrow and targeted: it does not change police practices, funding, or use-of-force rules, it only adds a federal criminal penalty for conduct that would already be murder or manslaughter if committed by anyone else. The main honest objection is that it overlaps state law and covers only federally funded agencies, but its core purpose — giving federal prosecutors independent of local police departments a tool when local systems do not charge an officer — is real and significant for the families involved.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in February 2020 and sent to the House Judiciary Committee, it sat there without a hearing, markup, or floor vote until the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 6, 2020 by Rep. Hank Johnson of Georgia with 16 original co-sponsors, including House Majority Whip Jim Clyburn and Reps. Pressley, Tlaib, Rush, and Norton.
It was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the same day.
It attracted 51 co-sponsors, all House Democrats.
The full action history shows no further action after the referral: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Police officers and their unions are better off because the bill died, since they avoid a new federal criminal charge for on-duty killings and assaults. Local prosecutors and police departments also avoid federal prosecutors competing with them over officer-involved deaths.

for.name: Rep. Jim Clyburn and 15 other original co-sponsors

against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee where the bill was referred, never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill shows no committee action after referral.

sides.party_line_note: All 52 sponsors and co-sponsors were House Democrats; no Republican supported the bill, and it never reached a floor vote where the parties' splits could be measured.

industries.industry: Law enforcement officers and police unions
industries.note: The bill would create federal murder and manslaughter liability for on-duty conduct by officers in federally funded agencies. Police unions and officers generally resist new criminal exposure for use of force, and the bill's death preserves the status quo in which officer-involved deaths are handled almost entirely by state and local systems.

By adding a parallel federal charge, the bill would let federal prosecutors bring homicide cases against officers even when local prosecutors decline. Its failure leaves charging decisions over officer-involved deaths exclusively with local systems.
